tip: For an action still going on, Russian uses the present with уже (uzhe = already): ждём уже двадцать минут (zhdyom uzhe dvadtsat minut = have been waiting twenty minutes).
Animate masculine accusative copies the genitive form: этого человека (etava chelaveka = this person), because a person is the object, not этот человек (etat chelavek).
назад (nazad = ago) comes after the time span, not before it: пять лет назад (pyat let nazad = five years ago).
covered with uses the instrumental with no preposition: покрыта снегом (pakryta snegam = covered with snow), no separate word for with.
поздравляю (pazdravlyayu = congratulations) takes с plus the instrumental: с повышением (s pavysheniyem = on the promotion).
Dates usually put day and month in the genitive: восьмого марта (vasmova marta = the eighth of March), literally of-the-eighth of-March.
домой (damoy = homeward) already means 'to home', so it needs no preposition and no case change.
Motion onto a surface takes на plus accusative: на стол (na stol = onto the table). Resting on it would be на столе (na stale).
мне жаль (mne zhal = I'm sorry) uses a dative person plus жаль, with no verb for 'to be'.
The verb поможет (pamozhet = will help) takes a dative object, so друг (drug) becomes другу (drugu = to a friend).
Wishing someone something uses genitive: удачи (udachi = good luck), a shortened form of 'I wish you luck'.
через (cherez = in) plus accusative sets a time from now: через час (cherez chas = in an hour).
The verb мечтает (mechtaet = dreams) takes о plus prepositional: о красивом доме (o krasivam dome = about a beautiful house).
по (pa = along) plus dative traces movement over a surface: по набережной (pa naberezhnay = along the embankment).
Part-words take the genitive: часть денег (chast' deneg = part of the money), and ушла (ushla) agrees feminine with часть.
After a quantity word the counted noun goes genitive plural: килограмм яблок (kilagramm yablak = a kilo of apples).
Some masculine nouns take a stressed -у in the location case: саду (sadu = in the garden), from сад (sad), not саде (sade).
The prefix в- (v-) adds inward motion: вошёл (vashyol = went in), while plain шёл (shyol) just means was walking.
с (s = with) plus instrumental gives manner here: с удовольствием (s udavolstviem = with pleasure, gladly).
The verb играет (igraet = plays) takes в plus accusative for games: в шахматы (v shahmaty = chess).
встречались (vstrechalis = met) ends in a reflexive -сь (-s), which with a plural subject reads as reciprocal: they met each other.
Russian good wishes use the genitive: хорошего полёта (harosheva palyota = of a good flight), literally wishing you 'of a good flight'.
нужна (nuzhna = needed) agrees with the thing needed, not the person: помощь (pomashch = help) is feminine, so нужна, not нужен.
к (k) means toward and takes the dative: к остановке (k astanovke = up to the stop). Use it for approaching a point.
With понравился (panravilsya = was liked), the liker goes dative, друзьям (druzyam = to friends), and the verb agrees with the thing liked, дом (dom = house).
вкусно готовят (vkusna gatovyat) has no subject, literally 'they cook deliciously'; Russian leaves out the 'they', which English turns into 'the food is delicious'.
идём (idyom = we go) is for going on foot; ехать (yehat = go by vehicle) is for vehicles. Russian marks how you travel, English uses 'go' for both.
Быть (byt) drops its present tense in everyday speech, but its future is regular: всё будет хорошо (vsyo budet harasho = all will be fine).
несколько (neskalka = several) takes the genitive plural: несколько студентов (studentav = of students). Quantity words govern the genitive.
по-русски (pa-russki = in Russian) is how you name a language of speech: по- plus the adverb, hyphenated and lowercase, never capitalized.
